opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a great question, and I think it's one of the most interesting open problems right now. Math and coding were the natural starting points because they have very clean verifiers. For a math problem you can check whether the final answer matches, and for code you can run unit tests. That gives you a reliable reward signal without needing a learned reward model that the policy can game.

Beyond those domains, I see a few directions.

The first is finding other domains that have some form of checkable outcome even if they aren't strictly math. Think of chemistry or physics problems with numerical answers, logic puzzles, formal theorem proving with something like Lean, structured data extraction where you can compare against a schema, or tool-use tasks where you can tell whether the API call succeeded and returned the right result. Agentic tasks are interesting here because the environment itself becomes the verifier: did the agent actually complete the task in the sandbox or not?

The second is softer verification, where you use rubrics or LLM-as-a-judge setups. That's where it gets trickier. Once your verifier is itself a model, you reintroduce the reward-hacking problem that made people excited about verifiable rewards in the first place. But in practice I think we'll see hybrid approaches: decompose an open-ended task into checkable pieces where possible, like "did it cite the source correctly" or "does it satisfy these constraints," and then use a judge only for the remaining fuzzy parts.

Third, there's a transfer question that I find really interesting. Even if you only train with verifiable rewards on math and code, some of the reasoning behaviors seem to carry over: breaking problems into steps, checking intermediate results, backtracking when something looks off. So part of "expanding beyond math and coding" may happen implicitly, because the habits learned there generalize somewhat to other tasks. How far that goes is still an empirical question, though.

I'd add one caveat. Not every task benefits from long reasoning chains. For simple factual questions or creative writing, more thinking tokens don't necessarily help and can just make things slower and more expensive. So I don't think the goal is to turn everything into a reasoning problem. It's more about identifying where verification is possible and where step-by-step reasoning actually adds value, and focusing the training there.

r001.rationale: The response says reasoning habits learned through verifiable rewards on math and code can carry over to other tasks.

r002.rationale: It discusses transfer and training in other domains, but does not say that training in a target domain benefits reasoning there more than math training alone.

r003.rationale: It does not propose rewarding molecular generation for complying with physical constraints.

r004.rationale: It does not question whether molecular generation constitutes reasoning.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's a question I think about a lot, because math and coding are in some sense the easy cases. You have a verifier that's essentially free and reliable. The answer either matches or it doesn't, the unit tests pass or they don't. That's what made the DeepSeek-R1 recipe work so cleanly: you can run RL with a simple rule-based reward and the model learns to produce those long reasoning chains without anyone having to annotate the intermediate steps.

The challenge is that most things people actually want to use these models for don't have that property. If I ask a model to summarize a paper or write a code review or give medical advice, there's no exact-match reward I can compute.

So I see a few directions. One is what I'd call "partially verifiable" domains. Even if the final output isn't checkable, pieces of it are. In scientific writing, for example, you can check that cited claims actually appear in the cited source, that numbers are internally consistent, that units line up. In data analysis, you can check that the code runs and produces the table the model claims it produces. You're not verifying the whole thing, but you're giving a much denser, more reliable signal than a preference model alone.

The second direction is using models as verifiers, which is where a lot of the work is going right now. The important nuance is that verification is often an easier problem than generation. It's easier to check a proof than to write one, easier to spot that an argument has a gap than to construct a complete argument. So even if your verifier model isn't perfect, there's an asymmetry you can exploit. The risk, of course, is reward hacking. If the verifier is a learned model, the policy will find its weaknesses. We've seen that with regular RLHF reward models, and it doesn't go away just because you call it a verifier.

The third one, which I think is underrated, is simulation and environments. For agentic tasks, instead of asking "was this answer correct," you ask "did the agent actually accomplish the goal in the environment." Did the file get created, did the booking go through, did the state of the system end up where it should. That's verification too, it just happens to be defined by the environment rather than a ground-truth label.

And honestly, I'd add a caveat. I think there's a temptation to assume the math-and-code recipe will just transfer with the right reward design. I'm somewhat skeptical of that. Part of why reasoning training works so well there is that the problems are self-contained and the chain of thought genuinely helps. For a lot of open-ended tasks, it's not obvious that more "thinking" helps in the same way, and we've seen cases where longer reasoning actually makes the output worse or more verbose without being more correct. So I think the expansion will be real, but it'll be more domain-by-domain engineering than one clean generalization.

r001.rationale: The response questions whether math-and-code reasoning training will transfer cleanly and does not claim it improves reasoning beyond mathematics.

r002.rationale: It favors domain-by-domain engineering, but does not say training reasoning in a target domain benefits that domain more than math reasoning training alone.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention molecular generation or using physical constraints as a training reward.

r004.rationale: The response does not discuss whether molecular generation constitutes reasoning.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is: How do we get a reliable feedback signal? Math and coding are convenient because you can check an answer or run a test. But the broader idea doesn’t require a mathematical answer. It requires some way to judge whether the model accomplished the task.

For example, if a model is using tools or interacting with an environment, you can check whether it reached the desired state. Did it successfully make the requested change? Did it satisfy the constraints? That gives you something you can train against, even if there are many valid ways to get there.

It becomes harder with open-ended tasks, like writing or giving advice, where quality is subjective. You can use another model to provide feedback, but then you’re relying on that model’s judgment, and it can have blind spots. The model you’re training might also learn to exploit those.

So I expect expansion first into tasks where at least parts of the outcome are checkable. You don’t necessarily need to verify every step of the reasoning, but you do need a feedback signal that actually reflects the behavior you want. Designing that signal is probably the biggest challenge.

r001.rationale: The response discusses expanding verification-based training beyond math, but does not say that training on math improves reasoning in other domains.

r002.rationale: It does not compare target-domain training with math training or claim that target-domain training benefits reasoning more.

r003.rationale: It gives no proposal involving molecular generation or physical constraints as a reward.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss whether molecular generation constitutes reasoning.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is: Can we check whether an answer is good without having to generate the ideal answer ourselves? Math and coding are convenient because you can check a result or run unit tests. But that idea can extend to other domains where we have constraints, simulations, or feedback from an environment.

Take a tool-using assistant. Did it actually complete the task? Did it produce a valid schedule that satisfies all the constraints? Those are things you can potentially verify. In science, you might check a prediction against a simulator or experimental data, although that feedback can be much more expensive.

The challenge is that a verifiable outcome isn’t always the same as a good outcome. If your verifier only checks part of the task, the model can learn to exploit that. So I expect progress first in tasks with fairly clear success criteria, and then in more open-ended tasks using a combination of verifiable checks and human judgment. The verifier becomes a really important part of the training system.

r001.rationale: The response says verification-based training could extend to other domains, but does not suggest that training on math problems improves reasoning beyond mathematics.

r002.rationale: It does not compare domain-specific reasoning training with math reasoning training alone.

r003.rationale: It mentions constraints in general, but does not propose using physical constraints as a reward for molecular generation.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss molecular generation or question whether it constitutes reasoning.
